arXiv:1507.00601v2 [gr-qc] 25 Apr 2016

The C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Schwarzschild spacetime and the spacelike diameter in Lorentzian geometry

Jan Sbierski ††thanks: Department for Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics, University of Cambridge, Wilberforce Road, Cambridge, CB3 0WA, United Kingdom
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The maximal analytic Schwarzschild spacetime is manifestly inextendible as a Lorentzian manifold with a twice continuously differentiable metric. In this paper, we prove the stronger statement that it is even inextendible as a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric. To capture the obstruction to continuous extensions through the curvature singularity, we introduce the notion of the spacelike diameter of a globally hyperbolic region of a Lorentzian manifold with a merely continuous metric and give a sufficient condition for the spacelike diameter to be finite. The investigation of low-regularity inextendibility criteria is motivated by the strong cosmic censorship conjecture.

1 Introduction

A connected Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g) is called CkC^{k}-inextendible, if there does not exist a connected Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) (of the same dimension as MM) with a CkC^{k}-regular metric g~\tilde{g} in which MM isometrically embeds as a proper subset. In this paper we prove:

Theorem.

The (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional maximal analytic Schwarzschild spacetime is C0C^{0}-inextendible for all d≥3d\geq 3.

The interest of the study of low-regularity inextendibility criteria for Lorentzian manifolds stems from the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in general relativity, which was conceived by Penrose and states, in physical terms, that, generically, the theory of general relativity should uniquely predict the fate of all local (classical) observers. A widely accepted mathematical formulation of this conjecture is the following:

(1.1) For generic asymptotically flat initial data for the vacuum Einstein equations R​i​c​(g)=0Ric(g)=0, the maximal globally hyperbolic development is inextendible as a suitably regular Lorentzian manifold.

However, there is still no consensus on the exact meaning of ‘suitably regular’ (and neither is there on the exact definition of ‘generic’ - but in the following we focus on the question which regularity class one should impose). In a series of papers [2], [3], [4], Christodoulou proved a corresponding formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system. He showed that ‘generically’, the maximal globally hyperbolic development is C0C^{0}-inextendible in the class of spherically symmetric Lorentzian manifolds11 1 However, no argument is given which would show the C0C^{0}-inextendibility in the class of Lorentzian manifolds without symmetry assumptions.. This very strong form of inextendibility of the maximal globally hyperbolic development is, however, particular to the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system: in [7], [8], Dafermos showed that for solutions to the spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system, arising from initial data close to that of the Reissner-Nordström solution, the maximal globally hyperbolic development is in fact C0C^{0}-extendible. Moreover, he showed that ‘generically’, the Hawking mass blows up which implies inextendibility as a spherically symmetric Lorentzian manifold with Christoffel symbols locally in L2L^{2}.

Recently, Dafermos and Luk announced the C0C^{0}-stability of the Kerr-Cauchy horizon (without any symmetry assumptions), [9]. More precisely, they show that for initial data on the event horizon, which approach the geometry of the Kerr event horizon in a manner compatible with the expected behaviour of the Kerr exterior under generic perturbations, the solution exists all the way up to the Cauchy horizon ‘in a neighborhood of timelike infinity’, and, moreover, is continuous and C0C^{0}-close to the unperturbed Kerr solution. This result, together with the expected stability of the Kerr exterior, shows that the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (1.1) does not hold if one imposes the strong C0C^{0}-inextendibility on the maximal globally hyperbolic development22 2 However, the result of Dafermos and Luk does not rule out the possibility that some part of the generic singularity inside a black hole is indeed C0C^{0}-inextendible.. So what regularity should one choose in the mathematical formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (1.1)?

Let us recall that the physical motivation of the conjecture is the belief in determinism in classical physics. Until one has gained a better understanding for the regime in which the classical theory of gravity needs to be replaced by a quantum theory, it seems sensible, in order to do justice to the physical content of the conjecture, to rule out non-unique extensions of the maximal globally hyperbolic development as, possibly weak, solutions to the Einstein equations. Such non-unique extensions could be constructed from a local existence result for the Einstein equations. Hence, this suggests that one should at least require inextendibility of the maximal globally hyperbolic development in all regularity classes which admit a local existence result for the Einstein equations (in a weak form). In the light of the recent low-regularity existence results, [12], [16], this regularity class is, in particular, below C2C^{2}.

The currently favoured formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, introduced by Christodoulou in [5], is to require generic inextendibility as a Lorentzian manifold with Christoffel symbols locally in L2L^{2}, since this even rules out the mere formulation of the Einstein equations (in a weak form). Moreover, the results [7], [8] by Dafermos lend support to the veracity of this version of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture.

It now seems, however, that the methods developed so far for proving inextendibility of Lorentzian manifolds have not penetrated regularities lower than C2C^{2} (or C1,1C^{1,1}).33 3 That is, if one disregards the spherically symmetric case where one can use the behaviour of the radius and the Hawking mass of the spheres of symmetry in a straightforward way as obstructions. Most of the known inextendibility results exploit geodesic completeness or the blow-up of curvature scalars as obstructions to C2C^{2}-extensions.

The aim of this paper is to initiate the study of low-regularity extensions of Lorentzian manifolds. In particular we show how one can use the infiniteness of the timelike diameter of the exterior of the Schwarzschild spacetime together with the infiniteness of a newly introduced geometric quantity, called the spacelike diameter, in the interior, to show that the maximal analytic Schwarzschild spacetime is C0C^{0}-inextendible. Although, as explained above, the singularity structure of the Schwarzschild solution is not expected to be generic, it is nevertheless an important and instructive illustrative model in general relativity. Furthermore, we feel that the techniques developed in this paper might also be helpful for further physically more relevant investigations.

1.1 C0C^{0}-extendibility and C2C^{2}-inextendibility

There are various examples of Lorentzian manifolds which are C2C^{2}-inextendible while being C0C^{0}-extendible. The physically most relevant example is probably given by the spacetimes constructed by Dafermos in [7], [8]. Another, very simple, example is provided by the Lorentzian manifold ((0,∞)×ℝ,g)\big((0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R},g\big), where the Lorentzian metric gg is given by

g=e2​t​(−d​t2+d​x2).g=e^{2\sqrt{t}}\big(-\,dt^{2}+dx^{2}\big)\;.

Clearly, this Lorentzian manifold can be continuously extended to [0,∞)×ℝ[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}. On the other hand, the scalar curvature of gg is found to be R=−12​e2​t⋅1t3/2R=-\frac{1}{2e^{2\sqrt{t}}}\cdot\frac{1}{t^{\nicefrac{{3}}{{2}}}}, which shows that no C2C^{2}-extension to [0,∞)×ℝ[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R} is possible.

Let us also briefly remark that there have been attempts to deduce from the strength of a curvature singularity whether it forms an obstruction to C0C^{0}-extensions or not. The example [18] by Ori of a strong curvature singularity which admits a C0C^{0}-extension showed, however, that the relation of these two concepts is not as straightforward as originally expected.

While there is an abundance of examples of C2C^{2}-inextendible Lorentzian manifolds, we are not aware, however, of any previous results showing C0C^{0}-inextendibility of a Lorentzian manifold. In particular, the methods presented in this paper can be used to show that the toy-example (M,g)(M,g), where M=ℝ×(0,∞)M=\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty) and

g=1h⁡(r)​d​t2−h⁡(r)​d​r2,g=\frac{1}{h(r)}\,dt^{2}-h(r)\,dr^{2}\,,

is C0C^{0}-inextendible. Here, tt is the coordinate on ℝ\mathbb{R}, rr the coordinate on (0,∞)(0,\infty), and h⁡(r)h(r) is a smooth and monotonically increasing function with h⁡(r)=rh(r)=r for 0<r<120<r<\frac{1}{2} and h⁡(r)=1h(r)=1 for r≥1r\geq 1.

1.2 Sketch of the proof

In the following we give a brief sketch of the proof of the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Schwarzschild spacetime. We refer the reader unfamiliar with any notation or definition in the following overview to Section 2 (and Section 4 for the definition of the Schwarzschild spacetime).

One assumes that there is a C0C^{0}-extension ι:Mmax↪M~\iota:M_{\mathrm{max}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of the maximal analytic Schwarzschild spacetime MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}} (in this overview we will not distinguish between MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}} and ι⁡(Mmax)⊂M~\iota(M_{\mathrm{max}})\subset\tilde{M}). Lemma 2.17 shows that there is then a timelike curve γ~\tilde{\gamma} in M~\tilde{M} leaving the Schwarzschild spacetime MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}}. This timelike curve can only ‘leave through’ either the curvature singularity at {r=0}\{r=0\}, or timelike or null infinity. These two cases are separately discussed and ruled out. Here, an important ingredient is Lemma 2.4, which introduces near-Minkowskian coordinates in a neighbourhood U~\tilde{U} of the point in the boundary of MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}}, through which γ~\tilde{\gamma} leaves MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}}. In particular, by estimating the future and pasts of points in U~\tilde{U} by cones with respect to the chosen coordinates, we can choose s0s_{0} such that the closure of I+​(γ~​(s0),U~)∩I−​(γ~​(0),U~)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),\tilde{U}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(0),\tilde{U}\big) in M~\tilde{M} is contained in U~\tilde{U}.

The important next step in deriving a contradiction is to identify subsets of U~\tilde{U} with subsets in MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}}. Let us remark here, that this step would be much simpler in Riemannian geometry, since one could use the distance function to do so.

We first discuss the case that γ~\tilde{\gamma} leaves MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}} through timelike or null infinity. Without loss of generality, we can assume that γ~\tilde{\gamma} is future directed in MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}}. Ideally, we would like to have the following identification for all s0<s<0s_{0}<s<0:

(1.2) I+​(γ~​(s0),U~)∩I−​(γ~​(s),U~)=I+​(γ~​(s0),Mmax)∩I−​(γ~​(s),Mmax).I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),\tilde{U}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s),\tilde{U}\big)=I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big)\;.

However, since on the left we consider a causality relation with respect to a small neighbourhood of M~\tilde{M}, and on the right with respect to MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}}, such an identification is not justified in general (and indeed, neither of the two inclusions is)! Here, however, we exploit that the exterior of the Schwarzschild black hole is future one-connected, i.e., in particular, any future directed timelike curve in MmaxM_{\mathrm{max}} from γ~​(s0)\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}) to γ~​(s)\tilde{\gamma}(s) is homotopic to γ~|[s0,s]\tilde{\gamma}|_{[s_{0},s]} via timelike curves with fixed endpoints. Since the closure of I+​(γ~​(s0),U~)∩I−​(γ~​(0),U~)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),\tilde{U}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(0),\tilde{U}\big) in M~\tilde{M} is contained in U~\tilde{U}, a homotopy as above cannot escape I+​(γ~​(s0),U~)∩I−​(γ~​(0),U~)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),\tilde{U}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(0),\tilde{U}\big). This yields the relation `​`⊇"``\supseteq" in (1.2). A contradiction is now obtained since the timelike diameter of I+​(γ~​(s0),U~)∩I−​(γ~​(s),U~)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),\tilde{U}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s),\tilde{U}\big) is bounded for s↗0s\nearrow 0, while the timelike diameter of I+​(γ~​(s0),Mmax)∩I−​(γ~​(s),Mmax)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0}),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big)\cap I^{-}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(s),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big) grows beyond bound for s↗0s\nearrow 0.

In order to show that γ~\tilde{\gamma} cannot leave through {r=0}\{r=0\} either, we introduce the spacelike diameter of a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold NN with a C0C^{0}-regular metric, defined by

Theorem.

Let (N,g)(N,g) be a connected and globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold with a C0C^{0}-regular metric gg and let ψk:Uk→Dk=⋃x¯∈BkIx¯×{x¯}\psi_{k}:U_{k}\to D_{k}=\bigcup_{\underline{x}\in B_{k}}I_{\underline{x}}\times\{\underline{x}\}, k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, be a finite collection of regular flow charts for NN with ⋃1≤k≤KUk=N\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq K}U_{k}=N.

Then one has diams​(N)<∞\mathrm{diam}_{s}(N)<\infty.

For the proof, one first notes that since there are finitely many charts that cover NN, it suffices to show that for each kk the diameter of Σ∩Uk\Sigma\cap U_{k} is uniformly bounded for all Cauchy hypersurfaces Σ\Sigma of NN. To establish the uniform bound, we show that ψk​(Σ∩Uk)\psi_{k}(\Sigma\cap U_{k}) can be written as a graph over BkB_{k} with uniformly bounded slope. Together with the uniform boundedness of the metric components, one obtains that the components of the induced metric on Σ∩Uk\Sigma\cap U_{k} are uniformly bounded (independently of the Cauchy hypersurface). This, together with the finiteness of the diameter of BkB_{k} then implies the uniform bound on the diameter of Σ∩Uk\Sigma\cap U_{k}.

Assuming now that γ~\tilde{\gamma} leaves through {r=0}\{r=0\}, we consider a near-Minkowskian neighbourhood U~\tilde{U} as before. One now has to show that there is a μ>0\mu>0 such that I+​(γ~​(−μ),Mmax)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(-\mu),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big) is contained in U~\tilde{U}. One then considers a spherically symmetric globally hyperbolic region NN as depicted above and shows that the spacelike diameter of NN is infinite. Here, one exploits that the coefficient of d​t2dt^{2} in the standard form (4.2) of the Schwarzschild metric diverges for r→0r\to 0.

The contradiction will be obtained from the above theorem. First note, however, that I+​(γ~​(−μ),Mmax)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(-\mu),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big) is not spherically symmetric, and hence, NN is actually not completely contained in I+​(γ~​(−μ),Mmax)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(-\mu),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big). The above representation is, however, accurate if one fixes a point on the sphere and only depicts the corresponding t,rt,r-plane. In particular, it holds that an open angular segment of NN is completely contained in I+​(γ~​(−μ),Mmax)I^{+}\big(\tilde{\gamma}(-\mu),M_{\mathrm{max}}\big). The near-Minkowskian chart for U~\tilde{U} can now be used to construct a regular flow chart for NN that covers an open angular segment of NN. Using the spherical symmetry of the Schwarzschild spacetime we can rotate this regular flow chart to obtain a collection of regular flow charts that cover NN. The above theorem now applies and yields the contradiction.

1.3 Further applications and open questions

In the following we collect a few more applications of the techniques developed in this paper and compile some open problems in the realm of C0C^{0}-extensions of Lorentzian manifolds.

  1. i)

    The timelike diameter can also be used as an obstruction to show that the de Sitter spacetime is C0C^{0}-inextendible. The proof proceeds along the same steps outlined in the first half of the above sketch (and in more detail in Section 3), where one can exploit, for example, the conformal isometry of de Sitter space with part of the Einstein static universe in order to prove a) the future one-connectedness of de Sitter space and b) the infiniteness of the timelike diameter of the intersection of the past of a future directed timelike curve ‘leaving’ de Sitter space with the future of an arbitrary point along the same curve.

    Other straightforward applications of the methods presented in this paper should be to the proof of the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter spacetime, Nariai, and Plebański-Hacyan - to name a few.

  2. ii)

    An interesting direction of research is regarding the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of cosmological spacetimes with a big bang singularity - and in particular the FRW models. A clarification of the obstruction to C0C^{0}-extensions through the initial singularity would, in particular, shed more light on the structure of the singularity. Here, new techniques are needed. An exception is the Kasner solution with a negative pip_{i}, which seems to be amenable to the methods developed in this paper, since the spacelike diameter near the singularity is diverging.

  3. iii)

    Another direction for further research is to leave the class of exact solutions and prove that the spacetimes constructed by Christodoulou in the series of papers [2], [3], [4], and which arise from the generic spherically symmetric collapse of a scalar field, are C0C^{0}-inextendible even if one leaves the class of spherically symmetric Lorentzian manifolds.

  4. iv)

    As already mentioned in the introduction, timelike geodesic completeness implies, in a straightforward way, the C2C^{2}-inextendibility of the Lorentzian manifold. However, this method of proof does not give C0C^{0}-inextendibility. An interesting question is whether there are examples of (timelike) geodesically complete Lorentzian manifolds which are C0C^{0}-extendible.

1.4 Outline of the paper

Section 2 collects the notions in causality theory we are using in this paper and presents a few basic, but important results on causality theory for continuous metrics. As a warm-up, we begin by proving the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Minkowski spacetime in Section 3, before we introduce the Schwarzschild spacetime in Section 4 and give the first half of the proof of its C0C^{0}-inextendibility. Thereafter, we introduce the notion of the spacelike diameter in Section 5 and give a sufficient criterion for it being finite. This notion is crucial to the second half of the proof of the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the maximal analytic Schwarzschild spacetime, which is presented in Section 6.

2 Definitions and aspects of causality theory for Lorentzian manifolds with continuous metrics

In this section, we compile the definitions of concepts in causality theory used in this paper. Moreover, we extend a few standard results in causality theory for a more regular Lorentzian metric to the case of a merely continuous Lorentzian metric.

All manifolds considered in this paper are Hausdorff, second countable, and of dimension d+1≥2d+1\geq 2. Moreover, note that for MM to carry a continuous Lorentzian metric, we need to assume that MM is at least endowed with a C1C^{1} differentiable structure. This, however, implies that one can find a compatible smooth differentiable structure on MM.44 4 See for instance [11]. In fact, one can even extend any smooth structure (which is compatible with the C1C^{1} structure) on a subset of MM to a smooth structure (compatible with the C1C^{1} structure) on all of MM. Hence, we will assume that all manifolds in this paper are smooth. This is for convenience only and not actually needed anywhere.

2.1 The timelike future remains open and consequences thereof

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric. Recall that a tangent vector X∈Tp​MX\in T_{p}M is called timelike, null, spacelike if, and only if, g⁡(X,X)<0g(X,X)<0, g⁡(X,X)=0g(X,X)=0, g⁡(X,X)>0g(X,X)>0, respectively. The set of all timelike vectors in Tp​MT_{p}M forms a double cone and, thus, has two connectedness components. One says that (M,g)(M,g) is time orientable if, and only if, one can find a continuous timelike vector field on MM. A choice of timelike vector field singles out one of the connectedness components and, thus, determines a time orientation.

Definition 2.1.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric. A piecewise smooth curve γ:I→M\gamma:I\to M, where I⊆ℝI\subseteq\mathbb{R} is connected, is called a timelike curve if, and only if, for all s∈Is\in I, where γ\gamma is differentiable, we have γ˙​(s)\dot{\gamma}(s) is timelike, and at each point of II, where the right-sided and left-sided derivative do not coincide, they are still both timelike and lie in the same connectedness component of the timelike double cone in the tangent space.

Definition 2.2.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric.

  1. 1.

    A timelike curve γ:I→M\gamma:I\to M is called future (past) directed if, and only if, its (one-sided) tangent vector is future (past) directed at some point of II (and hence at all points of II).

  2. 2.

    For two points p,q∈Mp,q\in M we define p≪qp\ll q (p≫qp\gg q) to mean that there exists a future (past) directed timelike curve from pp to qq.

  3. 3.

    For a point p∈Mp\in M, we define the timelike future I+​(p,M)I^{+}(p,M) of pp in MM by {q∈M|p≪q}\{q\in M\;|\;p\ll q\}. The timelike past I−​(p,M)I^{-}(p,M) of pp is defined analogously.

Remark 2.3.

In the setting of the above definition, where (M,g)(M,g) is a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric, consider an open subset U⊆MU\subseteq M. Note that (U,g|U)(U,g|_{U}) is a Lorentzian manifold in its own right, and in particular the future I+​(p,U)I^{+}(p,U) of a point p∈Up\in U is defined with respect to the causality structure of the manifold (U,g|U)(U,g|_{U}), and not with respect to the causality structure of the ambient manifold MM. Hence, there might be a point q∈Uq\in U which can be connected to pp via a past directed timelike curve lying in MM, which, however, cannot be connected to pp via a past directed timelike curve lying entirely in UU.

Although not needed in this paper, let us also remark that we do not make the relation ≪\ll smaller by imposing that a timelike curve should be piecewise smooth, since we can always smooth out a piecewise less regular timelike curve and, at the same time, preserve its causal character. However, this smoothing argument does not apply to causal curves! It is an easy exercise to write down a merely continuous Lorentzian metric in 1+11+1 dimensions, which does not admit a single smooth null curve.

Let us also mention at this point that there are results in the causality theory for smooth metrics which do not carry over to the merely continuous case. An instructive example in [6] shows that there are continuous Lorentz metrics for which the light cones are no longer hypersurfaces. In this paper, however, the only result in causality theory for merely continuous metrics we need is that the timelike future and past remains an open set. The proof of this statement is given below.

The following basic, but important, lemma introduces a near-Minkowskian coordinate system adapted to a timelike curve.

Lemma 2.4.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric gg, and let γ:[−1,0]→M\gamma:[-1,0]\to M be a timelike curve. After a possible reparametrisation of γ\gamma, we can find for every δ>0\delta>0 an open neighbourhood UU of γ⁡(0)\gamma(0), an ε>0\varepsilon>0, and a coordinate chart φ:U→(−ε,ε)d+1\varphi:U\to(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} such that

  1. 1.

    φ⁡(γ⁡(0))=(0,…,0)\varphi\big(\gamma(0)\big)=(0,\ldots,0)

  2. 2.

    (φ∘γ)​(s)=(s,0,…,0)(\varphi\circ\gamma)(s)=(s,0,\ldots,0) holds for s∈(−ε,0]s\in(-\varepsilon,0]

  3. 3.

    gμ​ν​(0)=mμ​νg_{\mu\nu}(0)=m_{\mu\nu}

  4. 4.

    |gμ​ν​(x)−mμ​ν|<δ\big|\,g_{\mu\nu}(x)-m_{\mu\nu}\,\big|<\delta holds for all x∈(−ε,ε)d+1x\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1}

are satisfied, where

mμ​ν=(−101⋱01)m_{\mu\nu}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&&&0\\ &1&&\\ &&\ddots&\\ 0&&&1\end{pmatrix}

is the Minkowski metric on ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}.

Proof.

Possibly after a linear change of parameter for γ\gamma, we can assume without loss of generality, that

(2.5) g​(γ˙​(0),γ˙​(0))=−1g\big(\dot{\gamma}(0),\dot{\gamma}(0)\big)=-1

holds. Since γ\gamma has only finitely many discontinuities, we can find a neighbourhood UU of γ⁡(0)\gamma(0) and a ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that γ((−ε,0])⊆U\gamma\big((-\varepsilon,0]\big)\subseteq U and γ|(−ε,0]\gamma\big|_{(-\varepsilon,0]} is smooth. Choosing UU and ε\varepsilon smaller if necessary, we can find a coordinate chart φ:U→(−ε,ε)d+1\varphi:U\to(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} such that the first two points of the lemma are satisfied55 5 More explicitly, we can choose coordinates ψ\psi which are centred at γ⁡(0)\gamma(0) and such that γ˙0​(0)≠0\dot{\gamma}_{0}(0)\neq 0. Hence, γ0−1\gamma^{-1}_{0} exists in a small enough neighbourhood and we set F⁡(x0,x¯)=(γ−1​(x0),x¯−γ¯​[γ0−1​(x0)])F(x_{0},\underline{x})=\big(\gamma^{-1}(x_{0}),\underline{x}-\underline{\gamma}[\gamma_{0}^{-1}(x_{0})]\big), which is a diffeomorphism in a small enough neighbourhood of 00. It then follows that (F∘ψ)(F\circ\psi) is a chart satisfying the first two points.. After a linear change of coordinates, obtained from the Gram-Schmidt orthonormalisation procedure based at the origin, where we keep ∂∂x0\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{0}} fixed (which is normalised by (2.5)), we can moreover arrange that, in addition, the third point holds. For given δ>0\delta>0, we can now choose UU and ε\varepsilon even smaller such that the fourth point of the lemma holds as well. This follows from the continuity of the Lorentz metric gg. ∎

Proposition 2.6.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric gg. For all p∈Mp\in M the timelike future I+​(p,M)I^{+}(p,M) and the timelike past I−​(p,M)I^{-}(p,M) of pp are open in MM.

We show that I+​(p,M)I^{+}(p,M) is open in MM; the proof of I−​(p,M)I^{-}(p,M) being open is analogous. So let q∈I+​(p,M)q\in I^{+}(p,M) and let γ:[−1,0]→M\gamma:[-1,0]\to M be a future directed timelike curve from pp to qq. By Lemma 2.4, we can find, after a possible reparametrisation of γ\gamma, a chart φ:U→(−ε,ε)d+1\varphi:U\to(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} such that 1. - 4. of Lemma 2.4 are satisfied with δ=12\delta=\frac{1}{2}. It follows that there exists a τ>0\tau>0 such that

∂∂x0+τ1​∂∂x1+τ2​∂∂x2+…+τd​∂∂xd\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{0}}+\tau_{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}+\tau_{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}+\ldots+\tau_{d}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{d}}

is timelike for |τi|<τ|\tau_{i}|<\tau, 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d. Thus, there exists a ball Bρ​(0)B_{\rho}(0) such that every point x∈Bρ​(0)x\in B_{\rho}(0) can be connected to (−ε2,0,…,0)(-\frac{\varepsilon}{2},0,\ldots,0) by a straight line which is timelike. Concatenating γ|[−1,−ε2]\gamma|_{[-1,-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}]} with the image curve of the straight line under φ\varphi shows that φ−1​(Bρ​(0))⊆I+​(p,M)\varphi^{-1}\big(B_{\rho}(0)\big)\subseteq I^{+}(p,M).

∎

The next two propositions are easy consequences of Proposition 2.6.

Proposition 2.7.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric gg. Let γ:[0,1]→M\gamma:[0,1]\to M be a future directed timelike curve. Then the following holds:

I−​(γ⁡(1),M)=⋃0≤s<1I−​(γ⁡(s),M).I^{-}\big(\gamma(1),M\big)=\bigcup_{0\leq s<1}I^{-}\big(\gamma(s),M\big)\;.
Proof.

The inclusion “⊇\,\supseteq\,” is clear. In order to prove “⊆\,\subseteq\,”, let q∈I−​(γ⁡(1),M)q\in I^{-}\big(\gamma(1),M\big). Hence, it follows that γ⁡(1)∈I+​(q,M)\gamma(1)\in I^{+}(q,M). By Proposition 2.6, I+​(q,M)I^{+}(q,M) is open and thus contains γ⁡(s)\gamma(s) for ss close enough to 11. This shows that q∈I−​(γ⁡(s),M)q\in I^{-}\big(\gamma(s),M\big) for ss close enough to 11. ∎

Proposition 2.8.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric gg, and let TT be a smooth and globally timelike vector field on MM.

For every p∈Mp\in M there exists a chart φ:U→(−Δ,Δ)×(−E,E)d\varphi:U\to(-\Delta,\Delta)\times(-E,E)^{d} centred at pp, where UU is an open neighbourhood of pp in MM, and Δ,E>0\Delta,E>0, such that

We call such a chart φ\varphi, which satisfies i) a flow chart, and if it satisfies i) and ii), we call it a flow chart with timelike connected orbits.

Proof.

Since TT is a regular vector field, the first part of the proposition is a standard result - see for example Theorem 17.13 in [15]. In order to prove the second statement, recall from Proposition 2.6 that I+​(0,(−Δ,Δ)×(−E,E)d)I^{+}\big(0,(-\Delta,\Delta)\times(-E,E)^{d}\big) and I−​(0,(−Δ,Δ)×(−E,E)d)I^{-}\big(0,(-\Delta,\Delta)\times(-E,E)^{d}\big) are open. Thus, we can choose E>0E>0 smaller such that, firstly, for every x¯∈(−E,E)d\underline{x}\in(-E,E)^{d} we can find an x0+∈[0,Δ)x_{0}^{+}\in[0,\Delta) such that (x0+,x¯)∈I+​(0,(−Δ,Δ)×(−E,E)d)(x_{0}^{+},\underline{x})\in I^{+}\big(0,(-\Delta,\Delta)\times(-E,E)^{d}\big), and secondly, we can find an x0−∈(−Δ,0]x_{0}^{-}\in(-\Delta,0] such that (x0−,x¯)∈I−​(0,(−Δ,Δ)×(−E,E)d)(x_{0}^{-},\underline{x})\in I^{-}\big(0,(-\Delta,\Delta)\times(-E,E)^{d}\big).

Hence, any two orbits of TT in the chart φ\varphi can be connected (via 00) by a future as well as a past directed timelike curve. ∎

2.2 Definitions

This section lays down more terminology used in this paper.

Definition 2.9.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric gg.

  1. 1.

    We define the Lorentzian distance function d⁡(⋅,⋅):M×M→[0,∞]d(\cdot,\cdot):M\times M\to[0,\infty] by

    d(p,q)={0 if ​q∉I+​(p,M)supσ:[0,1]→M​ future directedwith ​σ​(0)=p​ and ​σ​(1)=q{∫01−g​(σ˙​(s),σ˙​(s))ds} if ​q∈I+​(p,M)d(p,q)=\begin{cases}0&\textnormal{ if }q\notin I^{+}(p,M)\\ \sup\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma:[0,1]\to M\textnormal{ future directed}\\ \textnormal{with }\sigma(0)=p\textnormal{ and }\sigma(1)=q\end{subarray}}\Big\{\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{-g\big(\dot{\sigma}(s),\dot{\sigma}(s)\big)}\,ds\Big\}\qquad&\textnormal{ if }q\in I^{+}(p,M)\end{cases}

    Here, L⁡(σ):=∫01−g​(σ˙​(s),σ˙​(s))​𝑑sL(\sigma):=\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{-g\big(\dot{\sigma}(s),\dot{\sigma}(s)\big)}\,ds is also called the Lorentzian length of the timelike curve σ\sigma.

  2. 2.

    We define the timelike diameter of MM by diamt(M):=sup{d(p,q)|p,q∈M}\mathrm{diam}_{t}(M):=\sup\{d(p,q)\;|\;p,q\in M\}.

Definition 2.10.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric, and let I⊆ℝI\subseteq\mathbb{R} be one of the following intervals (a,b)(a,b), (a,b](a,b], [a,b)[a,b), or [a,b][a,b], where a<ba<b. A future directed timelike curve γ:I→M\gamma:I\to M is said to be future (past) extendible if, and only if, γ\gamma can be extended to I∪{b}I\cup\{b\} (I∪{a}I\cup\{a\}) as a continuous curve. Otherwise, γ\gamma is called future (past) inextendible. Moreover, we call γ\gamma inextendible if, and only if, γ\gamma is future and past inextendible.

Remark 2.11.

Note that the notion of future (past) extendibility of timelike curves only requires the extendibility of the timelike curve as a continuous curve. It thus may well happen that a timelike curve is future extendible, but we can not extend it to the future as a timelike curve.

Definition 2.12.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric.

  1. 1.

    We call a smooth embedded hypersurface Σ\Sigma of MM a Cauchy hypersurface in (M,g)(M,g) if, and only if, Σ\Sigma is met exactly once by every inextendible timelike curve.

  2. 2.

    We say that a Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g) is globally hyperbolic if, and only if, there exists a Cauchy hypersurface Σ\Sigma in (M,g)(M,g).

Definition 2.13.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric.

  1. 1.

    Two future directed timelike curves γi:[0,1]→M\gamma_{i}:[0,1]\to M, i=0,1i=0,1, with γ0​(0)=γ1​(0)\gamma_{0}(0)=\gamma_{1}(0) and γ0​(1)=γ1​(1)\gamma_{0}(1)=\gamma_{1}(1) are called timelike homotopic with fixed endpoints if, and only if, there exists a continuous map Γ:[0,1]×[0,1]→M\Gamma:[0,1]\times[0,1]\to M such that Γ⁡(t,⋅)\Gamma(t,\cdot) is a future directed timelike curve from γ0​(0)\gamma_{0}(0) to γ0​(1)\gamma_{0}(1) for all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and, moreover, Γ⁡(0,⋅)=γ0​(⋅)\Gamma(0,\cdot)=\gamma_{0}(\cdot) and Γ⁡(1,⋅)=γ1​(⋅)\Gamma(1,\cdot)=\gamma_{1}(\cdot). The map Γ\Gamma is also called a timelike homotopy with fixed endpoints between γ0\gamma_{0} and γ1\gamma_{1}.

  2. 2.

    We say that (M,g)(M,g) is future one-connected if, and only if, for all p,q∈Mp,q\in M, any two future directed timelike curves from pp to qq are timelike homotopic with fixed endpoints.

The following concept plays an important role in the proof of Theorem 4.11.

Definition 2.14.

Given two sets A,B⊆MA,B\subseteq M, we say that AA and BB are timelike separated by a set K⊆MK\subseteq M if, and only if, every timelike curve connecting AA and BB intersects KK - i.e., for any timelike curve σ:[0,1]→M\sigma:[0,1]\to M with σ⁡(0)∈A\sigma(0)\in A and σ⁡(1)∈B\sigma(1)\in B there exists an s0∈[0,1]s_{0}\in[0,1] with σ⁡(s0)∈K\sigma(s_{0})\in K.

If KK is a closed set, then M∖KM\setminus K is again a Lorentzian manifold. In this case, we clearly have that AA and BB are timelike seperated by KK if, and only if, I+​(A,M∖K)∩B=∅I^{+}(A,M\setminus K)\cap B=\emptyset and I−​(A,M∖K)∩B=∅I^{-}(A,M\setminus K)\cap B=\emptyset.

2.3 Extensions of Lorentzian manifolds

In the following we will tacitly assume that all manifolds are connected.

Definition 2.15.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a smooth metric gg.

  1. 1.

    Let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. A CkC^{k}-extension of (M,g)(M,g) is a smooth isometric embedding ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of MM into a proper subset66 6 Since we have tacitly assumed that all manifolds are connected, this implies ι⁡(M)¯∖ι⁡(M)≠∅\overline{\iota(M)}\setminus\iota(M)\neq\emptyset. of a Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}), where M~\tilde{M} is of the same dimension as MM, and g~\tilde{g} is a CkC^{k}-regular metric.

    By slight abuse of terminology, we sometimes also call M~\tilde{M} the extension of MM.

  2. 2.

    The Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g) is called CkC^{k}-extendible if, and only if, there exists a CkC^{k}-extension of (M,g)(M,g). Otherwise, (M,g)(M,g) is called CkC^{k}-inextendible.

Remark 2.16.
  1. 1.

    Of course, the question of extendibility is also of physical interest for Lorentzian manifolds (M,g)(M,g) which do not have a smooth metric gg. However, in this paper, the Lorentzian manifolds under consideration do have a smooth metric.

  2. 2.

    Note that we did not require in the definition of ‘extendibility’ that (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) is also time-orientable. However, this notion of ‘extendibility’ is not more general than if one imposed the condition of time-orientability on (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}). To see this, recall that every Lorentzian manifold has a time-orientable double cover77 7 See for example 17 Lemma in Chapter 7 of [17]., to which the isometric embedding can be lifted. However, we will not make use of this fact in this paper.

  3. 3.

    The notion of a Lorentzian manifold being extendible is global by nature. Although in Section 3.1 of [10] a definition to capture the idea of a ‘local extension’ was suggested, it was shown by Beem in [1] that it suffers from the shortcoming that the Minkowski spacetime then has to be considered as locally extendible.

The next Lemma shows that, given an extension, it is always possible find a timelike curve which leaves the original Lorentzian manifold.

Lemma 2.17.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with a smooth metric, let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, and let ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} be a CkC^{k}-extension of (M,g)(M,g). Then, there exists a timelike curve γ~:[0,1]→M~\tilde{\gamma}:[0,1]\to\tilde{M} such that γ~​([0,1))⊆ι​(M)\tilde{\gamma}\big([0,1)\big)\subseteq\iota(M) and γ~​(1)∈M~∖ι​(M)\tilde{\gamma}(1)\in\tilde{M}\setminus\iota(M).

Proof.

Since ι⁡(M)\iota(M) is a proper subset of the connected manifold M~\tilde{M}, its boundary ∂(ι⁡(M))\partial\big(\iota(M)\big) is non-empty. Let p~∈∂(ι⁡(M))\tilde{p}\in\partial\big(\iota(M)\big). We can find a small neighbourhood U~\tilde{U} of p~\tilde{p} that is time-oriented. Let q~∈I−​(p~,U~)\tilde{q}\in I^{-}(\tilde{p},\tilde{U}). We distinguish two cases:

  1. 1.

    q~∈ι⁡(M)\tilde{q}\in\iota(M): There exists a timelike curve γ~:[0,1]→U~\tilde{\gamma}:[0,1]\to\tilde{U} with γ~​(0)=q~\tilde{\gamma}(0)=\tilde{q} and γ~​(1)=p~\tilde{\gamma}(1)=\tilde{p}. Let

    s0:=sup{s∈[0,1]|γ~​([0,s))⊆ι⁡(M)}.s_{0}:=\sup\{s\in[0,1]\,|\,\tilde{\gamma}\big([0,s)\big)\subseteq\iota(M)\}\;.

    Since ι⁡(M)\iota(M) is open in M~\tilde{M}, it follows that γ~​(s0)∈M~∖ι⁡(M)\tilde{\gamma}(s_{0})\in\tilde{M}\setminus\iota(M). Reparametrising γ~|[0,s0]\tilde{\gamma}|_{[0,s_{0}]} then gives the timelike curve from the statement of the lemma.

  2. 2.

    q~∈M~∖ι⁡(M)\tilde{q}\in\tilde{M}\setminus\iota(M): Since I+​(q~,U~)I^{+}(\tilde{q},\tilde{U}) is open by Proposition 2.6 and contains p~∈∂(ι⁡(M))\tilde{p}\in\partial\big(\iota(M)\big), it must also contain a point r~∈ι⁡(M)\tilde{r}\in\iota(M). One now considers a timelike curve γ~:[0,1]→U~\tilde{\gamma}:[0,1]\to\tilde{U} with γ~​(0)=r~\tilde{\gamma}(0)=\tilde{r} and γ~​(1)=q~\tilde{\gamma}(1)=\tilde{q} and proceeds in analogy to the previous case.

∎

The importance of this lemma stems from the fact that it allows us to ‘locate’ the extension. By this we mean that we can choose a small neighbourhood U~\tilde{U} of γ~​(1)\tilde{\gamma}(1), which then gives us a region ι−1​(U~)\iota^{-1}(\tilde{U}) in the original manifold MM through which one extends. One can then start using the geometry of this region in MM to show that no such extension is possible. In particular, the lemma entails that if no timelike curve can leave MM, then MM must be inextendible.

The proof of the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Schwarzschild spacetime presented in this paper is by contradiction. Assuming that there is a C0C^{0}-extension, the above lemma implies that there must be a timelike curve leaving the Schwarzschild spacetime. It then follows, that such a timelike curve must either leave through the curvature singularity in the interior, or through timelike or null infinity in the exterior. Having located the possible extensions of the Schwarzschild spacetime, we then show that the timelike diameter being infinite in the exterior is a C0C^{0}-obstruction to extensions (however, one could also use the spacetime volume in a straightforward way as an obstruction), while in the interior, we show that the spacelike diameter being infinite forbids C0C^{0}-extensions.

As an instructive introduction to this scheme, we begin by proving the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Minkowski spacetime in the next section. In this case, we only need to capture the obstruction to C0C^{0}-extensions coming from the infiniteness of the timelike diameter of the Minkowski spacetime.

3 The C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Minkowski spacetime

Let d∈ℕ≥1d\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}. The (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime (MMink,m)(M_{\mathrm{Mink}},m) is given by the smooth manifold MMink=ℝd+1M_{\mathrm{Mink}}=\mathbb{R}^{d+1} together with the smooth Lorentzian metric m=−d​x02+d​x12+…+d​xd2m=-\,dx_{0}^{2}+\,dx_{1}^{2}+\ldots+\,dx_{d}^{2}, where (x0,x1,…,xd)(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}) are the canonical coordinates on ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}. The time orientation is fixed by stipulating that ∂∂x0\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{0}} is future directed.

A standard result in Lorentzian geometry is the C2C^{2}-inextendibility of the Minkowski spacetime. This follows from combining the fact, that for C2C^{2}-extensions, one can always find geodesics (even timelike ones) that leave the original Lorentzian manifold, together with the geodesic completeness of (MMink,m)(M_{\mathrm{Mink}},m).

Here, we establish the following

Theorem 3.1.

For every d≥1d\geq 1, the (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime (MMink,m)(M_{\mathrm{Mink}},m) is C0C^{0}-inextendible.

Proof.

The proof is by contradiction and proceeds in three steps.

Step 1: We assume that there exists a Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) with a continuous metric g~\tilde{g} and an isometric embedding ι:MMink↪M~\iota:M_{\mathrm{Mink}}\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} such that ι⁡(MMink)\iota(M_{\mathrm{Mink}}) is a proper subset of M~\tilde{M}. By Lemma 2.17, we can then find a timelike curve γ~:[−1,0]→M~\tilde{\gamma}:[-1,0]\to\tilde{M} such that γ:=ι−1∘γ~|[−1,0):[−1,0)→MMink\gamma:=\iota^{-1}\circ\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)}:[-1,0)\to M_{\mathrm{Mink}} is a timelike curve in MMinkM_{\mathrm{Mink}} and γ~​(0)∈M~∖ι⁡(MMink)\tilde{\gamma}(0)\in\tilde{M}\setminus\iota(M_{\mathrm{Mink}}). Without loss of generality we can assume that γ\gamma is future directed (otherwise reverse the time orientation), and hence it is future inextendible in MMinkM_{\mathrm{Mink}}.

Step 1.1: By Lemma 2.4, after a possible reparametrisation of γ~\tilde{\gamma}, there is an ε>0\varepsilon>0, an open neighbourhood U~⊆M~\tilde{U}\subseteq\tilde{M} of γ~​(0)\tilde{\gamma}(0), and a chart φ~:U~→(−ε,ε)d+1\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{U}\to(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} such that

  1. 1.

    (φ~∘γ~)​(s)=(s,0,…,0)(\tilde{\varphi}\circ\tilde{\gamma})(s)=(s,0,\ldots,0) holds for s∈(−ε,0]s\in(-\varepsilon,0]

  2. 2.

    |g~μ​ν​(x)−mμ​ν|<δ\big|\,\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu}(x)-m_{\mu\nu}\,\big|<\delta holds for all x∈(−ε,ε)d+1x\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} ,

where δ>0\delta>0 is small and to be fixed in the following.

Let 0<a<10<a<1 and let <⋅,⋅>Rd+1<\cdot,\cdot>_{R^{d+1}} denote the Euclidean inner product on ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} and |⋅|ℝd+1|\cdot|_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}} the associated norm. We introduce the following notation:

  • •

    Ca+:={X∈ℝd+1|<X,e0>ℝd+1|X|ℝd+1>a}C^{+}_{a}:=\big\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\,|\,\frac{<X,e_{0}>_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}{|X|_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}>a\big\}

    Ca−:={X∈ℝd+1|<X,e0>ℝd+1|X|ℝd+1<−a}C^{-}_{a}:=\big\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\,|\,\frac{<X,e_{0}>_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}{|X|_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}<-a\big\}

  • •

In Minkowski space, the forward and backward cones of timelike vectors correspond to the value a=cos⁡(π4)=12a=\cos(\frac{\pi}{4})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.

Since 58<12<56\frac{5}{8}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<\frac{5}{6}, we can now choose δ>0\delta>0 such that in the chart φ~\tilde{\varphi} from above all vectors in C5/6+C^{+}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{6}}} are future directed timelike, all vectors in C5/6−C^{-}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{6}}} are past directed timelike, and all vectors in C5/8cC^{c}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{8}}} are spacelike.

Step 1.2: We show that for x∈(−ε,ε)d+1x\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} we have the following inclusion relations

(3.2) I+​(x,(−ε,ε)d+1)⊆(x+C5/8+)∩(−ε,ε)d+1I−​(x,(−ε,ε)d+1)⊆(x+C5/8−)∩(−ε,ε)d+1.\begin{split}&I^{+}(x,(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1})\subseteq\big(x+C^{+}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{8}}}\big)\cap(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1}\\ &I^{-}(x,(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1})\subseteq\big(x+C^{-}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{8}}}\big)\cap(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1}\;.\end{split}

We only prove the first inclusion relation of (3.2), the second follows by reversing the time orientation. So let σ:[0,L]→(−ε,ε)d+1\sigma:[0,L]\to(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^{d+1} be a future directed timelike curve with σ⁡(0)=x\sigma(0)=x, and we impose that σ\sigma is parametrised by arc-length with respect to the Euclidean metric on ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}. Here, L=LEuclidean​(σ)>0L=L_{\mathrm{Euclidean}}(\sigma)>0 is the Euclidean length of the curve σ\sigma. Let us first assume that σ\sigma is smooth. We then compute

(3.3) <σ(L)−x,e0>ℝd+1|σ⁡(L)−x|ℝd+1=∫0L<σ˙​(s′),e0>ℝd+1​d​s′|σ⁡(L)−x|ℝd+1>58⋅L|σ⁡(L)−x|ℝd+1≥58,\frac{<\sigma(L)-x,e_{0}>_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}{|\sigma(L)-x|_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}=\frac{\int_{0}^{L}<\dot{\sigma}(s^{\prime}),e_{0}>_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}\,ds^{\prime}}{|\sigma(L)-x|_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}>\frac{5}{8}\cdot\frac{L}{|\sigma(L)-x|_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}}\geq\frac{5}{8}\;,

It now follows from (3.2) that we can choose s0∈(0,ε)s_{0}\in(0,\varepsilon) such that the closure of

4.1 The Schwarzschild spacetime

Let d∈ℕ≥3d\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}, m>0m>0, and r+:=(2​m)1d−2r_{+}:=(2m)^{\frac{1}{d-2}}. Moreover, we define D⁡(r):=1−2​mrd−2=1−r+d−2rd−2D(r):=1-\frac{2m}{r^{d-2}}=1-\frac{r_{+}^{d-2}}{r^{d-2}}.

The Schwarzschild exterior

Consider the smooth manifold Mext:=ℝ×((2​m)1d−2,∞)×𝕊d−1M_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\mathbb{R}\times\big((2m)^{\frac{1}{d-2}},\infty\big)\times\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, where m>0m>0 is a parameter. (4.1) gext=−(1−2​mrd−2)​d​t2+(1−2​mrd−2)−1​d​r2+r2​γ̊d−1,g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-\big(1-\frac{2m}{r^{d-2}}\big)\,dt^{2}+\big(1-\frac{2m}{r^{d-2}}\big)^{-1}\,dr^{2}+r^{2}\,\mathring{\gamma}_{d-1}\;,

The Lorentzian manifold (Mext,gext)(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}}) is called the exterior of a d+1d+1 dimensional Schwarzschild black hole with mass mm. It was introduced in 1916 in [19] by Schwarzschild for d=3d=3, where he also showed that it is a solution to the vaccum Einstein equations Ric⁡(g)=0\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0. In 1963, Tangherlini generalised Schwarzschild’s metric to higher dimensions, cf. [21].

4.2 The main theorem

Theorem 4.9.

This theorem can be easily deduced from the following two theorems:

4.3 Proof of Theorem 4.10

The proof of Theorem 4.10 proceeds in analogy to the proof of Theorem 3.1. However, we need to prove the analogous statement to Step 2 for the case of the Schwarzschild exterior. Step 2.1 will be replaced by Proposition 4.12, and Step 2.2 by Proposition 4.14.

Proposition 4.12.

The exterior of the Schwarzschild spacetime (Mext,gext)(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}}) is future one-connected.

Note that the proof of Step 2.1 for the Minkowskian case shows, in particular, that the Minkowski spacetime is future one-connected. Moreover, the proof given there can be transferred whenever the exponential map induces a global chart for the Lorentzian manifold. This, however, is clearly not the case for the Schwarzschild exterior.

5 The spacelike diameter in Lorentzian geometry

Theorem 5.3 of this section will be used in the proof of Theorem 4.11. The results of this section might, however, be also of independent interest. We begin by introducing the notion of the spacelike diameter, a geometric quantity at the level of C0C^{0}-regular Lorentzian metrics.

Definition 5.1.

Let (N,g)(N,g) be a connected and globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold with a C0C^{0}-regular metric gg. The spacelike diameter diams​(N)\mathrm{diam}_{s}(N) of NN is defined by

diams(N):=supΣ​ Cauchyhypersurface of ​NdiamΣ=supΣ​ Cauchyhypersurface of ​Nsupp,q∈Σinfγ:[0,1]→Σ piecewise smooth curvewith ​γ​(0)=p​ and ​γ​(1)=qL(γ).\mathrm{diam}_{s}(N):=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Sigma\textnormal{ Cauchy}\\ \textnormal{hypersurface of }N\end{subarray}}\mathrm{diam}\,\Sigma=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Sigma\textnormal{ Cauchy}\\ \textnormal{hypersurface of }N\end{subarray}}\sup_{p,q\in\Sigma}\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma:[0,1]\to\Sigma\\ \textnormal{ piecewise smooth curve}\\ \textnormal{with }\gamma(0)=p\textnormal{ and }\gamma(1)=q\end{subarray}}L(\gamma)\;.

Here, L⁡(γ)=∫01g​(γ˙​(s),γ˙​(s))​𝑑sL(\gamma)=\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{g\big(\dot{\gamma}(s),\dot{\gamma}(s)\big)}\,ds is the length of the curve γ\gamma. Note that this is well-defined since the tangent space of a Cauchy hypersurface Σ\Sigma does not contain timelike vectors.

Let us remark, that an attempt to capture the notion of a spacelike diameter in direct analogy to the Riemannian case, i.e., by considering shortest spacelike curves, clearly fails, since one can connect any two points by a spacelike curve of arbitrarily short length by using a nearly null zig-zag path.

Definition 5.2.

Let (N,g)(N,g) be a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold with a C0C^{0}-regular metric gg. A chart ψ:U→D\psi:U\to D for NN, where U⊆NU\subseteq N and D⊆ℝd+1D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, is called a regular flow chart for NN if, and only if

  1. 1.

    There exist constants C,cC,c such that the metric components in this chart satisfy the uniform bounds |gμ​ν|≤C<∞|g_{\mu\nu}|\leq C<\infty and g00≤c<0g_{00}\leq c<0.

  2. 2.

    The domain DD is of the form D=⋃x¯∈BIx¯×{x¯}⊆ℝ×BD=\bigcup_{\underline{x}\in B}I_{\underline{x}}\times\{\underline{x}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\times B, where B⊆ℝdB\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and Ix¯⊆ℝI_{\underline{x}}\subseteq\mathbb{R} is an open and connected interval. Moreover, the coordinate diameter diame​(B)\mathrm{diam}_{e}(B) of BB is finite, where diame​(B)\mathrm{diam}_{e}(B) is the diameter of B⊆ℝdB\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with respect to the standard Euclidean metric ee.

  3. 3.

    The timelike curves Ix¯∋s↦ψ−1​(s,x¯)I_{\underline{x}}\ni s\mapsto\psi^{-1}(s,\underline{x}) are inextendible in NN.

The following theorem is the main theorem of this section - it gives a sufficient criterion for the spacelike diameter to be finite.

Theorem 5.3.

Let (N,g)(N,g) be a connected and globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold with a C0C^{0}-regular metric gg and let ψk:Uk→Dk\psi_{k}:U_{k}\to D_{k}, k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, be a finite collection of regular flow charts for NN with ⋃1≤k≤KUk=N\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq K}U_{k}=N.

Then one has diams​(N)<∞\mathrm{diam}_{s}(N)<\infty.

Proof.

The proof is divided into two steps.

Step 1: For all Cauchy hypersurfaces Σ\Sigma of NN we have diam⁡(Σ)≤∑k=1Kdiam⁡(Σ∩Uk)\mathrm{diam}(\Sigma)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{diam}(\Sigma\cap U_{k}).

We then consider the open cover {(V1∪V2,⋃3≤k≤KVk}\{(V_{1}\cup V_{2},\bigcup_{3\leq k\leq K}V_{k}\} and proceed analogously. A finite number of iterations proves the claim.

Now assuming (5.4), we claim

(5.5) diam⁡(⋃1≤k≤mVk)≤∑k=1mdiam⁡(Vk) holds for all ​1≤m≤K.\mathrm{diam}\Big(\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq m}V_{k}\Big)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathrm{diam}(V_{k})\qquad\textnormal{ holds for all }1\leq m\leq K\;.

The proof is an induction in mm. For m=1m=1 there is nothing to show. Now assume (5.5) holds for m=m0<Km=m_{0}<K. Let p,q∈⋃1≤k≤m0+1Vkp,q\in\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq m_{0}+1}V_{k}. We need to show that the distance between pp and qq in ⋃1≤k≤m0+1Vk\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq m_{0}+1}V_{k} is bounded by the right hand side of (5.5). If p,q∈⋃1≤k≤m0Vkp,q\in\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq m_{0}}V_{k}, this follows by induction hypothesis. If p,q∈Vm0+1p,q\in V_{m_{0}+1}, this is trivial. It remains the case p∈⋃1≤k≤m0Vkp\in\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq m_{0}}V_{k} and q∈Vm0+1q\in V_{m_{0}+1} (or the other way around). By (5.4) there is a r∈(⋃1≤k≤mVk)∩Vm+1r\in\Big(\bigcup_{1\leq k\leq m}V_{k}\Big)\cap V_{m+1}. The triangle inequality then concludes the proof.

The next theorem is not needed for the proof of Theorem 4.11. However, its proof illustrates how an embedding of a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold NN into a larger Lorentzian manifold MM, such that NN is precompact in MM, allows us to construct regular flow charts for NN. Later, in the proof of Theorem 4.11, we morally encounter the more complex situation of finitely many embeddings of a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold NN into larger Lorentzian manifolds. The image of NN is not precompact in any of the larger manifolds, but taking all the embeddings into account, we can recover some sort of compactness and construct regular flow charts. This, however, is done ‘by hand’ in the proof of Theorem 4.11. Thus, the reader only interested in the proof of Theorem 4.11 can skip directly to Section 6.

Theorem 5.7.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time oriented Lorentzian manifold with a C0C^{0}-regular metric and N⊆MN\subseteq M an open and globally hyperbolic subset. Moreover assume that NN is precompact in MM and that ψ:ℝd⊇B2​(0)↪M\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\supseteq B_{2}(0)\hookrightarrow M is a smooth embedding of B2​(0)B_{2}(0) such that ψ|B1​(0):B1​(0)↪N⊆M\psi|_{B_{1}(0)}:B_{1}(0)\hookrightarrow N\subseteq M is a Cauchy hypersurface in (N,g)(N,g).

Then one has diams​(N)<∞\mathrm{diam}_{s}(N)<\infty.

Let us remark that we have assumed the existence of a global chart, and hence a trivial topology, of the Cauchy hypersurface for NN merely for simplicity of exposition. The reader is invited to write down more general formulations of this theorem.

Proof.

The proof is divided into three steps.

Step 1: The set-up.

Let us denote the maximal time interval of existence of the integral curve of TT in MM, starting at p∈Mp\in M, by Ip,MI_{p,M}. It follows that 𝒟=⋃p∈MIp,M×{p}\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_{p\in M}I_{p,M}\times\{p\}. Moreover let us define the maximal time interval of existence of the integral curve of TT in NN, starting at q∈Nq\in N, by Iq,NI_{q,N}.

Setting 𝒟ψ,2:=⋃x¯∈B2​(0)Iψ⁡(x¯),M×{x¯}⊆ℝ×B2​(0)\mathcal{D}_{\psi,2}:=\bigcup_{\underline{x}\in B_{2}(0)}I_{\psi(\underline{x}),M}\times\{\underline{x}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\times B_{2}(0), we define χ2:𝒟ψ,2→M\chi_{2}:\mathcal{D}_{\psi,2}\to M by

χ2​(s,x¯):=Φs​(ψ⁡(x¯)).\chi_{2}(s,\underline{x}):=\Phi_{s}\big(\psi(\underline{x})\big)\;.

χ1:=χ2|𝒟ψ,1:𝒟ψ,1→N\chi_{1}:=\chi_{2}|_{\mathcal{D}_{\psi,1}}:\mathcal{D}_{\psi,1}\to N

is a diffeomorphism. This is seen as follows:

  • •

    Surjectivity: Let p∈Np\in N. Since every integral curve of TT intersects Σ\Sigma only once, it follows that x¯0=x¯1\underline{x}_{0}=\underline{x}_{1}. Moreover, if s0≠s1s_{0}\neq s_{1}, then there is a closed integral curve of TT in NN, which contradicts the global hyperbolicity of NN. Thus, we have s0=s1s_{0}=s_{1}.
